skill.title: System Design
skill.summary: Scaling, caching, failure handling and the trade-offs between them.
skill.description: Reason about load, failure and consistency. State requirements, estimate capacity, and defend trade-offs between latency, cost and correctness.

questions.title: Scaling out behind a load balancer
questions.prompt: You want to run five identical instances of a web API behind a round-robin load balancer. Which property matters most for this to work without sticky sessions?

options.text: Each instance has its own local database
Instances keep no per-user state in memory; shared state lives in a database or cache
Each instance runs on a larger machine than before
The load balancer retries every failed request on all instances

questions.explanation: If an instance stores sessions or other per-user state in memory, the next request may land on an instance that doesn't have it. Keeping instances stateless, with shared state in a database or cache, lets any instance serve any request and lets you add or remove instances freely.
rubric: Identifies statelessness of application instances as the key property.
Explains what breaks when state is held in memory.
Places shared state in an external store.
misconceptions: Scaling out is the same as using bigger machines.
Each instance can safely own a separate copy of the data.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Identifies stateless instances with shared state kept in an external store.

questions.title: Cache-aside on a miss
questions.prompt: A service uses the cache-aside pattern with Redis in front of PostgreSQL. On a cache miss, what happens?

options.text: Redis fetches the row from PostgreSQL and stores it automatically
The application reads PostgreSQL, returns the value, and writes it to the cache
The request fails and the client retries after the cache warms
PostgreSQL pushes the row to Redis through a trigger

questions.explanation: In cache-aside (lazy loading) the cache is passive. The application checks the cache, loads from the source of truth on a miss, then populates the cache, usually with a TTL. This is different from read-through caching, where the cache itself loads missing data.
rubric: States that the application, not the cache, loads data on a miss.
Describes populating the cache after the read, typically with a TTL.
Distinguishes cache-aside from read-through caching.
misconceptions: Caches load missing data from the database on their own.
Cache misses are errors.

resources.title: AWS Builders' Library: Caching challenges and strategies

questions.acceptance_criteria: States the application loads from the database on a miss and then populates the cache.

questions.title: Why add jitter?
questions.prompt: Clients retry failed calls with exponential backoff. Why should the delays also include random jitter?

options.text: To make each retry more likely to succeed on its own
To spread retries out so many clients don't retry in synchronised waves
To hide retry behaviour from rate limiters
Jitter is only needed when there is a single client

questions.explanation: When many clients fail at the same moment, identical backoff schedules make them retry at the same moments, producing load spikes that can keep a recovering service down. Randomising delays spreads retries over time. Pair it with retry limits and timeouts.
rubric: Explains synchronised retries from many clients (the thundering herd).
States that jitter spreads load over time.
Mentions retry limits or retry budgets alongside backoff.
misconceptions: Retries are always safe to add.
Backoff alone prevents synchronised retry storms.

resources.title: AWS Builders' Library: Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter

questions.acceptance_criteria: Explains that jitter de-synchronises retries from many clients.

questions.title: Capacity for a URL shortener
questions.prompt: Estimate the storage and read throughput for a URL shortener that creates 10 million links per month, keeps them for five years, and serves 100 reads for every write. State your assumptions, then say which component you would scale first.
questions.hint: Work out writes per second first, then multiply. Round aggressively: the goal is the order of magnitude.
questions.explanation: Writes ≈ 10M / (30 × 86,400) ≈ 4 per second on average; reads ≈ 400 per second, with a peak multiplier on top. Five years ≈ 600M links; at ~500 bytes each that is roughly 300 GB before indexes and replication. The workload is read-heavy and highly cacheable, so a cache in front of the store is the first lever.
rubric: Converts monthly volume to an average per-second write rate.
Derives read throughput from the read/write ratio and considers peaks.
Estimates total storage from link count and a stated record size.
Identifies the read-heavy pattern and proposes caching first.
States assumptions explicitly.
misconceptions: Average load is enough for capacity planning.
Precise numbers matter more than stated assumptions.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Produces order-of-magnitude write, read and storage estimates from stated assumptions and identifies caching as the first lever.

questions.title: Stale data after an update
questions.prompt: A service uses cache-aside in front of PostgreSQL. After a user changes their display name, some pages show the old name for minutes. Explain the race conditions that can cause this and design an invalidation strategy, including its trade-offs.
questions.hint: Consider a read that misses the cache, loads the old value, and writes it back after the update has already invalidated the key.
questions.explanation: A slow reader can load the old row, the writer then updates the database and deletes the key, and the reader finally writes the stale value back, where it lives until the TTL expires. Prefer deleting keys over updating them on write, keep TTLs short as a safety net, and close the race with versioned values, leases, a delayed second delete, or change-data-capture–driven invalidation. Pages that need read-your-writes can bypass the cache for the current user.
rubric: Describes the reader–writer interleaving that repopulates a stale value.
Prefers invalidation (delete) over updating the cache on write, with reasoning.
Uses TTLs as a bound on staleness.
Proposes a mechanism such as versioning, leases, delayed double delete or CDC.
Handles read-your-writes requirements separately.
misconceptions: Deleting the cache key after a database write guarantees freshness.
Shorter TTLs alone eliminate stale reads.

resources.title: AWS Builders' Library: Caching challenges and strategies

questions.acceptance_criteria: Describes the stale-repopulation race and proposes a mechanism that bounds or prevents it.

questions.title: A popular key expires
questions.prompt: A product page's cached data expires every five minutes. At each expiry, database CPU spikes as thousands of requests miss the cache at once. Which change addresses the cause?
questions.hint: How many requests need to recompute the value?

options.text: Increase the TTL to one hour so expiries happen less often
Let one request rebuild the value while others wait or get the stale copy
Add a read replica so the database can absorb the spike
Disable caching for the product page, since it causes the spikes

questions.explanation: This is a cache stampede: many concurrent misses on one hot key all recompute the same value. Coalescing (a lock or single-flight so only one request rebuilds), serving stale data while refreshing in the background, or refreshing early with jitter all remove the burst. A longer TTL only spaces the stampedes out, and a replica adds capacity without changing the pattern.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “Let one request rebuild the value while others wait or get the stale copy”. This is a cache stampede: many concurrent misses on one hot key all recompute the same value.
rubric: Names the cache stampede.
Proposes request coalescing or serve-stale-while-refreshing.
Mentions early or jittered refresh as an option.
Explains why TTL changes and more capacity do not fix the cause.
misconceptions: Longer TTLs solve stampedes.
Stampedes are a database capacity problem.

questions.title: Sharding a multi-tenant database
questions.prompt: A SaaS product shards its database by `tenant_id`, which keeps each tenant's queries on one shard. One tenant is 200 times larger than the median and keeps growing. What is the main risk, and a reasonable mitigation?
questions.hint: Can one tenant's data be spread across several shards with this key?

options.text: Cross-shard joins for every query; denormalise all tables
A hot shard that cannot scale with that tenant; isolate or sub-shard large tenants
Uneven primary keys across shards; switch to UUIDs
Too many shards for small tenants; merge all small tenants into one database

questions.explanation: Sharding by tenant keeps queries local, but a single large tenant can outgrow any one shard and slow the neighbours sharing it. Common mitigations are placing very large tenants on dedicated shards, sub-sharding them by another key such as account or region, and keeping a directory that maps tenants to shards so they can be moved. Cross-shard joins are mostly avoided by this key choice, not caused by it.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “A hot shard that cannot scale with that tenant; isolate or sub-shard large tenants”. Sharding by tenant keeps queries local, but a single large tenant can outgrow any one shard and slow the neighbours sharing it.
rubric: Identifies the hot-shard risk from a skewed tenant.
Proposes dedicated or sub-sharded placement for large tenants.
Mentions a tenant-to-shard directory to allow moves.
Explains why tenant-based sharding avoids cross-shard joins.
misconceptions: Hash sharding always spreads load evenly.
Any shard key works if the number of shards is large.

questions.title: Availability of a request path
questions.prompt: Each request must succeed in both service A and service B. A is 99.9% available. B runs as two independent replicas, each 99.9% available, with perfect failover between them. Failures are independent. What is the approximate availability of the request path?
questions.hint: Calculate B's availability first, then combine it with A.
questions.explanation: Redundant replicas combine in parallel: B fails only if both replicas fail, 0.001 × 0.001 = 0.000001, so B is about 99.9999% available. Components on the path combine in series: 0.999 × 0.999999 ≈ 0.999, about 99.9%. The single copy of A now dominates. Real systems rarely have perfect failover or independent failures, so these numbers are upper bounds.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “99.9%”. Redundant replicas combine in parallel: B fails only if both replicas fail, 0.001 × 0.001 = 0.000001, so B is about 99.9999% available.
rubric: Combines B's replicas in parallel (1 − 0.001²).
Combines A and B in series by multiplying.
Arrives at about 99.9% and notes A dominates.
States the assumptions (independence, perfect failover) are optimistic.
misconceptions: Adding a replica doubles availability.
Availability of a path equals its weakest component exactly.

questions.title: A database overloaded by reads
questions.prompt: A product catalogue's PostgreSQL primary is at 90% CPU. About 95% of queries are reads of product pages, and a few seconds of staleness is acceptable. Which change helps most directly?
questions.hint: Which component is saturated, and by what kind of work?

options.text: Add read replicas and send product-page reads to them
Add more application servers behind the load balancer
Move writes to a second primary that accepts the same tables
Increase the connection pool size on every application server

questions.explanation: The bottleneck is read load on one database. Streaming replicas serve read-only queries, so routing tolerant reads to them spreads that load; a cache in front of hot pages would also help. More app servers or bigger pools add load to the same primary. Replicas do not scale writes, and replication lag means reads can be slightly stale, which this scenario allows.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “Add read replicas and send product-page reads to them”. The bottleneck is read load on one database.
rubric: Identifies read load on the primary as the bottleneck.
Routes stale-tolerant reads to replicas (or a cache).
Notes replicas do not scale writes and may lag.
misconceptions: More application servers scale the database.
Read replicas scale writes.

resources.title: PostgreSQL docs: High availability, load balancing and replication

questions.title: A burst of thumbnail requests
questions.prompt: Users upload photos in bursts of up to 5,000 per minute after events, while the thumbnail service can process 1,000 per minute and is idle most of the day. Requests currently call it synchronously and time out during bursts. What is the best design change?
questions.hint: Does the thumbnail need to exist before the upload request returns?

options.text: Put uploads on a durable queue and let workers drain it at a steady rate
Raise the client timeout to ten minutes so requests eventually succeed
Run five times the thumbnail capacity all day to cover the peak
Drop uploads that arrive while the service is busy and ask users to retry

questions.explanation: Queue-based load leveling decouples the upload from the slow work: the API stores the photo, enqueues a job and returns immediately, and workers process the backlog at their own rate, optionally autoscaling on queue depth. The burst becomes a temporary backlog instead of timeouts. Provisioning for the peak wastes money, long timeouts tie up connections, and dropping work hurts users.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “Put uploads on a durable queue and let workers drain it at a steady rate”. Queue-based load leveling decouples the upload from the slow work: the API stores the photo, enqueues a job and returns immediately, and workers process the backlog at their own rate, optionally autoscaling on queue depth.
rubric: Proposes an asynchronous queue between upload and processing.
Explains that bursts become a backlog rather than failures.
Mentions scaling workers on queue depth or eventual completion to users.
misconceptions: Every request must finish its work before responding.
Capacity must always match peak load.

resources.title: Azure Architecture Center: Queue-based load leveling pattern

questions.title: Adding one cache node
questions.prompt: A cache cluster of 10 nodes chooses a node with `hash(key) % N`. You add an 11th node. Roughly what fraction of keys now map to a different node, and what reduces it?
questions.hint: For how many keys does `hash % 10` equal `hash % 11`?

options.text: About 1/11; modulo hashing already moves only the new node's share
About 10/11; consistent hashing would move only about 1/11
None; existing keys stay where they are until they expire
All keys; any hashing scheme must remap everything when N changes

questions.explanation: With modulo hashing, a key stays put only if `hash % 10 == hash % 11`, which holds for roughly 1 in 11 keys, so about 10/11 move and the cache effectively empties. Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a ring (usually with many virtual nodes per server), so adding a node takes over only the keys between it and its neighbours: about 1/(N+1) of the total.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “About 10/11; consistent hashing would move only about 1/11”. With modulo hashing, a key stays put only if `hash % 10 == hash % 11`, which holds for roughly 1 in 11 keys, so about 10/11 move and the cache effectively empties.
rubric: Estimates that most keys move with modulo hashing.
Explains consistent hashing moves about 1/(N+1).
Mentions virtual nodes for balance.
misconceptions: Modulo hashing only moves keys to the new node.
Rehashing is unavoidable whenever the cluster changes.

resources.title: DeCandia et al.: Dynamo, Amazon's highly available key-value store
